challenges.title: Single Number
challenges.prompt:
In the list `nums`, every value appears exactly twice except one, which appears once. Return that value.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4, and the length is odd
Every value appears twice except exactly one
hints: A set or a counter solves it in O(n) space. Can you cancel the pairs instead of remembering them?
XOR has a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, and the order of operations does not matter.
XOR every number together, starting from 0. The pairs cancel and the single value is what remains.
challenges.explanation: XOR is commutative and associative, a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a. XOR-ing the whole list therefore cancels every pair, wherever its two copies sit, and leaves the value that appears once. It works for negative numbers in both languages, because the values fit in 32 bits.

challenges.title: Number of 1 Bits
challenges.prompt: Given a non-negative integer `n`, return how many 1 bits its binary representation has (its population count).
hints: You could test each of the 31 bits with (n >> k) & 1 and add them up.
Faster: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. How many times can you do that before n becomes 0?
Loop while n is not 0: n &= n - 1 and count one per pass.
challenges.explanation: Brian Kernighan's trick: n & (n - 1) removes exactly one set bit (the lowest), so the loop runs once per 1 bit instead of once per bit position. In Python, bin(n).count("1") or n.bit_count() (3.10+) also work. In JavaScript the operators work on 32-bit signed integers, which is fine here because n stays below 2^31.

complexity.time: O(number of set bits), at most 31 iterations

challenges.title: Counting Bits
challenges.prompt:
Given a non-negative integer `n`, return a list `ans` of length `n + 1` where `ans[i]` is the number of 1 bits in `i`, for every `i` from 0 to `n`.

Can you do it in one pass, in O(n) time overall?
hints: Counting each number's bits separately takes O(n log n). Can an answer you already have help?
i >> 1 is i with its last bit dropped, a smaller number whose count is already in the list.
ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Another option: ans[i] = ans[i & (i - 1)] + 1.
challenges.explanation: A tiny DP over the numbers themselves. Dropping the last bit (i >> 1) gives a smaller number whose count is already known, and i & 1 says whether the dropped bit was a 1. Each entry costs O(1), so the whole list takes O(n).

challenges.title: Power of Two
challenges.prompt:
Given an integer `n`, return `true` if it is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...), otherwise `false` (`True` or `False` in Python). Zero and negative numbers are never powers of two.

Can you do it without a loop?

examples.explain: 6 is 110 in binary: two bits are set.

hints: Write a few powers of two in binary. How many bits are set in each?
n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so it is 0 exactly when n has at most one set bit.
Remember the guard: 0 and negative numbers must return false. In JavaScript, parenthesize: (n & (n - 1)) === 0.

solution.python:
def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0

challenges.explanation: A positive power of two has exactly one set bit, and n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so the result is 0 only when that was the only bit. The n > 0 guard rejects 0 (where 0 & -1 is 0) and negative numbers such as -2^31, whose 32-bit pattern also has a single set bit. In JavaScript the parentheses matter, because === binds more tightly than &.
